here’s a short grok bot guide on how i create high quality bots and manage my team. ask @bot to read this post and help you improve your team!

• add dr eggbot to your team! he’s my bot designer that i use to create bots
• you don’t need a lot of bots. a few good bots can be more useful and easier to manage than a large team
• tell your bots to create skills for itself as you give it instructions on how to do tasks. this lets them do them more consistently even over long conversations. you can even ask it to create a private github repo for you to store all your skills if you want them preserved independently
• add connectors, use the vault, and give access to all the tools you use to do your work. you can also ask your bot to setup its own email and it can sign up for its own accounts for better separation
• thinking about all the work you do by hand, or steps in your workflows where you have to copy and paste information back to your bot. ask your bot how it can do that for you instead!
• imagine you hired an intern, how would you onboard them and help them do the work correctly and efficiently? introduce yourself to your bot and describe the work you do, then ask it how it can help you automate it

and my favorite tip: use voice mode or the transcription option! it’s a good way to just brain dump a lot of information. then, at the end, tell your bot to “restate this in your own words” so you can confirm it understood you

WAZOSKY@Imwazosky · Nov 1

A San Francisco biotech startup, Exin Therapeutics, hooked an AI agent to its motorized surgery rig, and the agent picked a gene therapy and operated on a live mouse's brain.

An AI agent just operated on a living mouse's brain. 🧠🤖

What happened:
1. Exin Therapeutics, a San Francisco biotech startup, hooked an AI agent up to its motorized surgery rig with cameras, says CEO @OcanaSantero.
2. The agent got 19 gene therapy vectors in a spreadsheet, a mouse model of epilepsy and one goal: reduce seizures. It picked the therapy, chose the brain region, worked out the coordinates and drove the needle, injecting 250 nanolitres.
3. The twist: Claude Opus 5.5 refused to do the live injection. The team switched to Claude Sonnet 5 (@claudeai, built by @AnthropicAI), which went ahead.
4. Humans stayed in the loop: a vet performed the craniotomy, approved every irreversible step and held a kill switch that cuts power to the rig's motors.
5. The mouse is reportedly recovering well. Whether the therapy reduces seizures is still pending, and nothing has been peer reviewed. Anthropic did not comment to WIRED.

Why it matters:
AI is moving from writing about experiments to physically running them. Agents with direct access to lab equipment could speed up research, but they also raise hard questions about oversight, refusals and who is accountable.

My take: the most interesting part isn't that the agent operated. It's that one model said no, and another refused to bypass its own safety limits mid-procedure. Guardrails are becoming part of the lab protocol.

Should AI agents be allowed to run live lab experiments? Reply with your take 👇

Xiao Huaxi | AI vs AI@xiaohuaxi28 · Oct 31

Two AI agents (Claude Code running Opus 5.5) built a 33-second Omaha Beach landing tribute entirely in Blender, with no video generation model.

Two AI agents built this 33-second tribute to the Omaha Beach landing in Saving Private Ryan, entirely in Blender, including the underwater bullet shot (0:12). No video generation models were used, and nothing in it comes from the film.

Claude Code running Opus 5.5 on high effort built the whole pipeline in one stretch. But Opus can't hear audio. It cut sound effects blind from vintage Hollywood sound libraries, and those old recordings open with a man announcing the take. So the waves at the start of its draft had a clear voice saying "Line FX 5 take 1!"

Right when it paused and asked me to listen to the clips myself, my Claude account got banned.

Gemini 4 Argon in Google Antigravity took over. Argon can listen, so it went through every clip and pulled out 5 of those voice slates. Checking rendered frames, it also turned the blocky first-draft soldiers, who looked like they wore flat UFO hats, into silhouettes with M1 helmets and packs. Then it caught the explosion lights leaving 5-meter round glare spots on the water like fried eggs. It swapped them for a volumetric fireball and a light with no mirror-like reflections, so the blasts still flash and the eggs are gone.

Under the hood, Python drives a live Blender window. Everything is modeled in code except two AI-generated backdrop textures. All 798 frames rendered in EEVEE on an M4 Mac. The sound is CC0 Freesound recordings synced to the animation frames where the ramp drops and each shell bursts.

A Claude Code tip from Anthropic: run Sonnet, Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5.5 together, each on the job it does best, for better results and fewer tokens.

THIS IS AN ACTUAL F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5.5 at once, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Better results and way fewer tokens, because every task lands on the right model.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session, writes the code and applies the fixes
→ Haiku 5.5 swarms the repo in parallel: search, grep and diff audits
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls and signs off on the diff
→ you stop burning Opus context on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku swarms. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and coordinates the work
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5, read-only
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5 in its own context
> audit checks the diff on Haiku 5.5 in a throwaway worktree
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reviews the synthesized diff before sign-off
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Reconfigure my Claude Code setup around this tree:
1. Run the main session on Sonnet 5.5 with Opus 5.5 as advisor.
2. Create three Haiku 5.5 subagents in .claude/agents: search (maps the repo), grep (finds call sites), audit (checks the diff).
3. Set isolation: worktree on audit so its checks never touch my working branch.
4. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: delegate every repo search and test run to the Haiku 5.5 subagents to keep the main context small.
5. Route fast deterministic forks (tool choice, path selection, retries) through JEV.
Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go."

↳ code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-ag…

save it, it'll come in handy.
